correctness.rationale: The unit-side embedding gives the exact face projection residual for every face, and swapping retained/omitted barycentric coordinates proves nearest support consists of the m largest. The ordered-chamber constant-density Jacobian gives a Dirichlet(1,...,1) gap vector. Substituting into the squared residual yields the explicitly simplified kernel 1/m-1/min(r,s). Its exact second Dirichlet moments yield the harmonic formula for all k>=2 and 1<=m<k, and the fixed-m, proportional-m and fixed-codimension limits follow from stated finite identities. The standalone source checker reproduced exact rational expectations for 66 parameter pairs, direct face comparisons and seven independently sampled estimates. Infinite claims rely on algebraic proof, not on finite tests.

originality.rationale: The 2012 sparse simplex projection source supplies the deterministic support-selection principle, which is explicitly credited. Its full-text Problem 1, Algorithm 1 and Theorem 1 do not state a Dirichlet random-input squared-error profile. Conway and Sloane (1982) calculate a fixed-centroid simplex inertia and lattice Voronoi quantization, not the nearest distance to each simplex skeleton. Existing identified research on skeleton Minkowski convexification and finite vertex averages addresses different operations. The accepted contribution is the evaluated simultaneous geometric mean-square profile in all dimensions, its joint Dirichlet quadratic-form representation, and its three asymptotic regimes. Searches do not establish absolute novelty; the reported conclusion is conditional on inspected literature and unresolved unindexed equivalence risk.

value.rationale: The mean squared distance to a simplex skeleton is a natural, dimension-dependent Euclidean approximation invariant, measuring error for all ranks of sparse barycentric approximation. The result completes a coherent full-skeleton profile, not an arbitrary finite slice: it gives a common joint Dirichlet law, exact values at every rank, and distinct constant, 1/k, and 1/k^4 scaling regimes. These exact quantitative benchmarks have plausible use in geometric quantization and sparse simplex projection, even without an asserted downstream theorem.
